outline.section: H2: What Actually Makes a Bar Soap Moisturizing?
outline.guidance: Explain the three core factors that determine whether a bar soap hydrates or strips skin: (1) glycerin retention — natural cold-process soap produces glycerin as a byproduct and retains it; many commercial bars remove it for other products; (2) superfatting — the percentage of oils left unsaponified in the bar that condition skin; (3) oil profile — the fatty acid composition of the base oils used (e.g., coconut oil adds lather and lauric acid, olive oil adds oleic acid for softness, shea adds stearic acid for barrier support). Keep this educational but accessible — no jargon without a plain-English explanation. Cite a credible source (dermatology or cosmetic chemistry) for the glycerin claim. This section is the key differentiator vs. competitors who skip the 'why.'

outline.section: H2: Bar Soap vs. Body Wash: Which Is Better for Moisture?
outline.guidance: Answer this directly because it is a real question in the audience's mind (body wash options surface heavily in related keywords). State the verdict up front: a well-formulated natural bar soap retains more glycerin than most body washes and produces less waste. Then give a brief, fair breakdown — body wash can carry more humectants like hyaluronic acid in suspension, but many are loaded with sulfates that strip skin; a high-quality natural bar soap with a good oil profile can outperform conventional body wash for dry skin. Link internally to the bar soap vs. liquid hand soap post. Do NOT create a competitor brand comparison table. Keep it a clear, confident recommendation toward natural bar soap without dismissing body wash entirely.

outline.section: H2: Key Ingredients to Look for in a Moisturizing Bar Soap
outline.guidance: Present this as a practical label-reading guide. Cover 5–6 ingredients that signal a genuinely moisturizing bar soap: (1) coconut oil — rich lather, antimicrobial lauric acid, (2) shea butter — occlusive, soothes irritation, (3) olive oil — high oleic acid, classic skin-softening oil, (4) castor oil — humectant, adds moisture-drawing properties, (5) glycerin — humectant, draws moisture to skin surface, (6) oat extract — soothing, ideal for sensitive or eczema-prone skin (address the Reddit eczema audience indirectly here without making medical claims). Briefly note what to avoid: sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), synthetic fragrance, parabens, artificial colors. This section directly addresses the 'what to look for on the label' gap in competitor content.

outline.section: H2: How to Use a Moisturizing Bar Soap to Get the Best Results
outline.guidance: Give 4–5 practical tips that maximize the moisturizing effect of a natural bar soap: (1) use lukewarm — not hot — water to avoid stripping natural oils; (2) lather in your hands or on a washcloth first, don't drag the bar directly on skin; (3) pat dry rather than rubbing; (4) apply a natural body lotion or coconut oil immediately after while skin is still slightly damp to lock in moisture; (5) store bar soap on a draining soap dish so it dries between uses and lasts longer. Keep this concise and actionable. Mention the body lotion application tip as a natural bridge to Real Skin Care's clean body lotion range if relevant.

outline.section: H2: Natural Bar Soap vs. Conventional Detergent Bars — What's the Difference?
outline.guidance: Clarify the key distinction that many searchers don't know: many products sold as 'bar soap' in mainstream retail are technically synthetic detergent bars (syndets) — they're not soap at all. They're made with surfactants like SLS rather than saponified oils, and they often have glycerin removed. True natural bar soap is made through saponification of real oils and retains naturally occurring glycerin. This distinction is critical for understanding why some bar soaps dry skin and others don't. Use this section to justify why choosing a natural, organic bar soap matters — and why Real Skin Care's formulations are built on real saponified oils, not synthetic detergents. Cite a cosmetic chemistry or dermatology source for the syndet claim.

Include 4 concise FAQ items formatted for FAQPage schema. Questions to cover: (1) 'Is bar soap good for dry skin?' — Yes, if it's a superfatted natural bar; explain briefly. (2) 'What ingredients make a bar soap moisturizing?' — Glycerin, shea butter, coconut oil, olive oil; brief answer pointing back to the ingredient section. (3) 'Is bar soap better than body wash for sensitive skin?' — Depends on formulation; natural bar soap with no SLS is often gentler. (4) 'Can I use moisturizing bar soap on my face?' — Some bars are suitable for facial use; look for bars without high coconut oil percentages (can be comedogenic for some) and without synthetic fragrance. Keep each answer to 2–4 sentences. Do not make absolute medical claims.
